title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open-source governance, risk, and compliance Risk and compliance people actually keep current RiskWren is one connected register of what an organization has, what could go wrong, what it must comply with, what it does about both, and the proof. It is built first for the security team: frameworks, assessments, findings, and exceptions are the path it gets right before anything else. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub

title: Overview
heading: Test once, satisfy many
text: A control is described once, mapped to every requirement it answers, and tested once. The result shows in every framework and every scope that relies on it.

title: Overview
heading: Worked out, never typed in
text: Readiness comes from tests and evidence that still count. Saying a control is in place never makes it verified, and what was verified decays by itself.

title: Overview
heading: Nobody marks their own work
text: A second person confirms a test result, the closure of an issue, and an exception. The server refuses anything else, whatever the role.

title: Overview
heading: Passive by design
text: No scanners, collectors, or agents, and no access to anything else on the network. It records what people know and decide. Readiness

title: Overview
heading: Where you stand against a framework, with the reason
text: A scope is a boundary held to one or more frameworks. Each requirement that applies in it is in exactly one of six states: verified, in place, excepted, planned, gap, or failing. Each control that answers it carries a sentence saying how it came to be there. When a central team's control fails a test, every scope that inherits it shows the failure the same day. How readiness is worked out Assessments

title: Overview
heading: A result counts when a second person confirms it
text: An assessment plans a test for each control a scope does itself. Nobody records or reviews a result for a control they own, and whoever recorded a result cannot confirm it. Once confirmed, the result becomes the control's rating, moves every requirement the control answers in every scope that relies on it, and moves the residual rating suggested for every risk it reduces. Assessments and tests Issues

title: Overview
heading: Every finding in one register, each with a date
text: A failed test opens an issue for the control's owners without anyone asking. Penetration tests, audits, incidents, and gaps go in the same register. Severity sets the date. Moving it needs a reason and stays on the record. An issue closes only when someone who does not own it confirms it was put right. Issues, from raised to closed Exceptions

title: Overview
heading: Exceptions that end by themselves
text: When a requirement cannot be met yet, the honest answer is an exception: why, what is done meanwhile, and the dates it runs between. Whoever asked does not decide. While it is in force the requirement shows as excepted, with the state underneath beside it. The day after it ends, that state is back. Nothing has to run for that to happen. Asking, deciding, and what follows Connections

title: Overview
heading: What is this connected to?
text: In an incident or a review the questions are always the same: what does this system support, which scopes is it in, what controls stand in front of it, and what is already known to be wrong with them. Every record opens to a picture of what it is joined to, with a list beside it that says the same in full. All of it works from the keyboard. Connections Risk

title: Overview
heading: Ratings you can read, decided by named people
text: Likelihood and impact have five levels, each with a written definition. Inherent, residual, and target ratings are judgments by named people, with reasons. The controls linked to a risk suggest a residual rating, and the suggestion opens to the arithmetic behind it. When a test moves it past the rating on record, the risk is flagged and its owner is asked to assess again. What the controls suggest Home

title: Overview
heading: One page of what each person owes
text: Most people who own a risk, a control, or an action are not risk professionals. Home lists what is theirs to do, each item a short task: a test to record, a result to confirm, an issue to put right, an exception about to end. A security leader's Home starts with the figures that cannot wait, such as controls failing a test and issues past their date, then the decisions that are theirs to make. Home

title: Overview
heading: Frameworks as published
text: NIST CSF 2.0, SP 800-53 Rev. 5 with its baselines, SP 800-171 Rev. 3, and the HIPAA Security Rule arrive loaded. An agreement or an internal standard is entered as a framework of your own.

title: Overview
heading: Inherited controls
text: A central team runs backup and identity once. Other scopes inherit those controls, and see a failure the day the provider's test finds it.

title: Overview
heading: Evidence that stops counting
text: Evidence is collected once and attached to everything it supports. Past its date it stays on the record and counts toward nothing.

title: Overview
heading: Working on the first day
text: A risk taxonomy, a scoring method, 57 common risks, and 75 common controls come with a new installation. The security controls among them arrive mapped to about three quarters of each framework.

title: Overview
heading: A history that holds
text: Every change is in an append-only, hash-chained log, with who made it. An auditor reads everything and changes nothing.

title: Overview
heading: Rating and standing
text: How much is at stake, and whether it is in order, are always two signals. Neither is told by color alone.

title: Overview
heading: In and out
text: Every list exports as CSV or JSON. Records come in from a spreadsheet, with a dry run that reports every problem by row.

title: Overview
heading: Who sees what
text: Roles are held over units. A figure never counts a record its reader could not open, and evidence is more closely held than the register.

title: Overview
heading: Open and yours
text: Apache 2.0 with no paid edition. SQLite on a laptop or PostgreSQL on a server, five runtime dependencies, and your own name and colors.

title: Overview
heading: Try it
text: You need uv , which provides the right Python. Clone the repository and build the demo organization: a fictional research institute with a clinic, two years of history, three scopes held to frameworks, an assessment in progress, evidence going stale, and issues and exceptions at every stage. git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/riskwren.git cd riskwren uv sync uv run riskwren demo uv run riskwren --config demo/riskwren.toml serve Open http://127.0.0.1:8020 . The sign-in page offers ten sample people and asks for no password. Start as the security leader. Explore the demo organization says who to try next, and Getting started sets up an installation of your own.

title: Overview
heading: Where it stands
text: These pages describe version 0.2.1: the register and compliance. It signs in with local accounts and sends no email; notices are in the app. Single sign-on, email, reminders, and attestations come next, then policies, supplier reviews, audits, and incidents. The roadmap says what comes in what order, and the changelog lists what is in each release.

title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from nothing to a running RiskWren that your organization can sign in to. It is for whoever installs it and sets it up. Allow about fifteen minutes. If you only want to look around first, skip to Explore the demo organization .

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: uv , which provides the right Python (3.12 or later). A copy of this repository. Every command in these guides is run through uv run riskwren … from the repository directory. The full list is in the command reference .

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: uv sync

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the installation
text: uv run riskwren init init does five things: Writes riskwren.toml , the deployment settings, in the current directory. Creates the data home, ./var , which holds everything that is not in the database. Creates the database. With no other setting, this is a SQLite file inside the data home. Loads the default program: nine families of risk with an appetite for each, a scoring method with defined scales, review cadences, the table of who may accept what, a library of 57 common risks, a library of 75 common controls, and four public frameworks (the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, and the HIPAA Security Rule) with the common controls already mapped

title: Getting started
heading: Check it
text: uv run riskwren doctor doctor checks the configuration, the data home, that the database answers, that its schema is the one this version expects, that the database still refuses changes to the history, and that the history verifies. It exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.

title: Getting started
heading: Run it
text: uv run riskwren serve The server prints its address, by default http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Use --port to pick another port. serve refuses to start in three cases, and says what to do in each: It says Do this The database schema is behind uv run riskwren db upgrade There is no administrator yet uv run riskwren users add you@example.org --name "Your Name" --role admin The port is already in use Stop what is using it, or pass --port As installed, RiskWren listens only on the machine it runs on. To put it in front of other people, read Configuration first.

title: Getting started
heading: Sign in for the first time
text: Open the address in a browser and sign in with the email address and password you gave init . This release signs in with local accounts: an email address and a password held by RiskWren. Single sign-on comes later; see the roadmap . Five failed attempts within fifteen minutes stop sign-in for that account from that address for a few minutes. A sign-in ends after 12 hours without activity, and after 7 days in any case. Both are settings . To change your password, open the account menu at the top right and choose Your account . Changing it signs out your other sessions. If you cannot sign in at all, reset the password from the command line: uv run riskwren users reset-password you@example.org

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the organization
text: The administrator account sets the installation up. It does not assess or accept risk: that belongs to the roles below, and an administrator who also does that work is given a second role.

title: Getting started
heading: Units
text: Admin → Units holds the organization as a hierarchy of any depth: divisions, departments, labs, cores, clinics, offices. Every record belongs to a unit, roles can be limited to a unit and everything beneath it, and figures roll up the tree. Give each unit a short code; imports and the command line refer to units by it.

title: Getting started
heading: People and roles
text: Admin → People adds accounts and gives them roles. A person with no role is a member: they see what they are named on, and their own unit's register if the program allows it. Role What it is for Manager The risk and compliance team. Edits any record, shapes the program, reads everything. Can be limited to a unit Assessor Assesses risks and rates controls they do not own. Can be limited to a unit Auditor Reads everything, including the full history, and changes nothing Leader Leads a unit. Sees it and everything beneath it, and may accept risk in it up to a limit set on the role Steward Keeps a unit's records: adds and edits its processes, systems, third parties, risks, and controls Admin Acc

title: Getting started
heading: Import units and people
text: Both screens take a CSV file, which is the quick way to load an organization. Each import can be run dry first and reports every problem by row, so nothing is half-loaded. The import dialog shows the columns it expects.

title: Getting started
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance sets the product's name, your organization's name, a logo, an accent color, the default palette, and how ratings are colored. See Running the program .

title: Getting started
heading: Explore the demo organization

Three scopes are held to frameworks: central information technology, which provides controls; the clinical systems, under the HIPAA Security Rule; and a controlled-access data enc

title: The register
heading: The register
text: The register This guide is for everyone who owns, assesses, or reads a risk. It covers the inventory, risks and their ratings, controls, what the controls suggest, treatment plans, and acceptance. What the organization is held to, and the proof that it meets it, is in Compliance . RiskWren is one connected register. A system is recorded once and every risk that concerns it points at it. A control is described once and every risk it bears on leans on the same record, with the same rating of how well it works.

title: The register
heading: Home
text: Home is the page for what you owe. Waiting on you lists, most urgent first, the things that need you in particular: an action that is yours, a risk of yours that has not been assessed or is due for review, a risk whose rating is in doubt, a risk that needs a decision, a control of yours to rate, an acceptance you gave that is about to expire, evidence of yours that has stopped counting or soon will, a test you have been asked to do, a result waiting for your review, an issue that is yours to put right, a closure waiting for you to confirm, an exception to decide or one of yours about to end, and, for those who can name a new owner, a record with nobody answering for it. Each item is a link t

title: The register
heading: The inventory
text: The inventory is what the organization has and depends on. It has four kinds of record: Record What it is Reference Process Something the organization does: a service a core provides, a clinical activity, payroll PRC-0001 System What the work runs on: an application, a platform, an instrument, a device, a data store SYS-0001 Third party Who it depends on: suppliers, service providers, collaborators, sponsors, subrecipients TP-0001 Information asset A body of information it holds: what it is, where it is kept, and who it is shared with. The record describes the information and never contains it INF-0001 Every record has a name, a unit, a criticality, the most sensitive class of data it touche

title: The register
heading: Links
text: A record says what it relies on: From Link To Process relies on System Process is performed by Third party System is supplied by Third party System holds Information asset Process uses Information asset Information asset is shared with Third party Process or system depends on · is part of Another of the same kind A link is made once, from either end, and can be read from both. A lab can say that its work relies on central storage without anyone in central computing doing anything.

title: The register
heading: Connections
text: Every record has a Connections link beside its name. It opens a picture of everything joined to the record: its links in both directions, the risks that bear on it, the controls that reduce them, the scopes it is in, and the evidence, issues, and exceptions about it. A list beside the picture says the same in full. See Connections .

title: The register
heading: Known elsewhere as
text: A record can carry what it is called in other systems: an asset tag, a contract number, a ticket, an entry in a configuration database. Known elsewhere as → Edit on the record. Search finds a record by any of them, and where the system has an address pattern they are links.

title: The register
heading: Import and export
text: Every list has an Export button. It gives the list as it is filtered, and as much of it as you may see, as a spreadsheet (CSV) or as data (JSON). Taking an export is recorded in the history. A steward or a manager can Import processes, systems, third parties, information assets, risks, and controls from a spreadsheet saved as CSV: Choose the file. RiskWren reads its headings and matches them to fields where the names make it plain. Say which column holds anything it could not match. A unit is given by its code or its name, an owner by their email address, and a choice by its key or by the words you see in the app. Check the file. Every problem is listed with its row. Nothing has been added y

title: The register
heading: Owners
text: Every record names the people who answer for it. An owner is accountable, a delegate acts for the owner day to day, and a contact knows the detail. Owners and delegates may edit the record. When an owner's account is disabled, the record is not reassigned by guesswork. It is shown as having nobody answering for it, on Home for those who can name a new owner, until someone does.

title: The register
heading: History
text: Every record has a History tab: who changed what, when, with each value before and after. Nothing in it can be edited or removed. See The history .

title: The register
heading: Raise a risk
text: Register → Raise a risk. Start from the library when you can, by searching it at the top of the form: it holds 57 common risks, written as a cause, an event, and a consequence, each with its category and the controls commonly used for it. Change the wording to fit; the library is a starting point, not a standard. A risk needs a name, a category, and a unit. Say what it concerns by linking the processes, systems, and third parties involved, so that anyone looking at a system sees the risks that bear on it.

title: The register
heading: Assess it
text: A risk carries up to three ratings, and each is a judgment recorded by a named person with a reason. Rating The question it answers Inherent How much is at stake if the controls did not exist or did not work? Residual How much remains, with the controls as they actually work? Target Where should it be once the plan is done? To assess, choose a likelihood from 1 (rare) to 5 (almost certain) and an impact from 1 to 5 on each dimension that applies: mission, safety, financial, legal, and trust. Every level has a written definition, shown as you choose, so that two people rating the same thing reach the same answer. The overall impact is the highest level on any dimension, and the rating is read

title: The register
heading: Rating and standing
text: These are two different things, and RiskWren always shows them apart. The rating says how much is at stake. The standing says whether the risk is in order. Standing Meaning Within appetite The residual rating is at or below what the organization has said it will live with for this kind of risk Being treated Above appetite, with a plan that is active and on time Accepted Above appetite, and accepted by someone with the authority, until a date Needs a decision Above appetite, and neither treated nor accepted. This is what leaders should look at Not assessed No residual rating yet Closed No longer applies, and kept for the record A critical risk that is accepted is in order. A moderate one in a

title: The register
heading: Reviews
text: Each risk has a next review date, sooner the more is at stake: by default every 3 months for critical, 6 for high, 12 for moderate, and 24 for low. A review is a new residual assessment, even when nothing has changed; say so in the reason. A risk past its date shows as overdue, on its page and on its owner's Home.

title: The register
heading: Escalate
text: A steward or leader can escalate a risk to a unit above its own, with a reason. The risk stays where it is and keeps its owner; escalation says "this needs you" to the leader above, and puts it among the risks at that level.

title: The register
heading: Close
text: Close a risk when it no longer applies, with the reason. It leaves the open register and stays findable, with its whole history.

title: The register
heading: Controls
text: A control is something the organization does to make a risk less likely or less harmful. It has a statement of what is done, an owner, a unit, a kind (preventive, detective, corrective, or directive), and how often it happens. Controls → Library is your organization's own controls. Add a control can start from a set of 75 common controls in plain words: search it, choose one, and then make it specific. The starting text says "backups are tested"; yours says which systems, how often, and by whom.

title: The register
heading: Rate a control
text: What is known about a control is recorded as a rating with two parts and a note: Design: if it were done as described, would it work? Operation: is it actually done? Each is effective, partly effective, or ineffective. The note says what was looked at. As with assessments, a rating is never edited, only superseded. A control that has never been rated is not assessed , and a rating older than twelve months is out of date . Neither counts for anything until someone looks. A rating by its owner or a steward is a judgment. A rating from a test in an assessment, recorded by someone who does not own the control and confirmed by a second person, outranks it: while a test result holds, the control c

title: The register
heading: Link a control to a risk
text: On the risk's Controls tab, link each control that bears on it and say how: what it reduces : likelihood, impact, or both; how much the risk leans on it: primary (the risk relies on it) or supporting (it helps). A risk started from the library offers the controls commonly used for it.

title: The register
heading: What the controls suggest
text: Once a risk has an inherent rating and linked controls, RiskWren shows the residual rating the controls suggest, with its working: Each control counts by how well it is known to work: effective counts in full, partly effective counts half, and ineffective, not assessed, and out of date count nothing. A primary control counts in full; a supporting one counts half. The counts are added up for likelihood and for impact. Each whole point takes that axis down one level, by at most two levels. So a critical risk at likelihood 4 and impact 5, with one primary control that works, one that partly works, and impact controls adding up to one, is suggested at likelihood 3 and impact 4: high. The suggest

title: The register
heading: When the picture changes
text: If a control is later rated worse, or unlinked, and what the controls now suggest is worse than both the residual rating on record and what was suggested when it was made, the risk is flagged: its rating is in doubt , with the reason named. RiskWren never changes a rating by itself. It asks the owner to assess again.

title: The register
heading: Treatment
text: A risk above appetite needs an answer. On the risk's Treatment tab, record the response , with the reason: reduce it, accept it, transfer it (by contract or insurance), or avoid it (by stopping the activity).

title: The register
heading: Plans and actions
text: A treatment plan says what will be achieved, who owns it, by when, and the rating it aims for. Its actions are the steps, each with an owner and a due date. While a plan is active and its date has not passed, the risk is being treated . An action's owner marks it in progress and done. Moving its date needs a reason, and the original date and every move stay on the record. When a plan's last action is done, the plan is complete. That does not lower the rating: the risk is flagged, and its owner is asked for a new residual assessment that reflects what was actually achieved. A plan that passes its date with work still open no longer counts, and the risk needs a decision again. Treatment plans

title: The register
heading: Accept a risk
text: Accepting a risk is a decision by a named leader to live with what remains, for a stated reason, until a date. Three rules always hold: Nobody accepts a risk they own. It goes to a leader above. Only a leader of the risk's unit, or of a unit above it, may accept it, and for a high or critical risk only one whose limit reaches that rating. An acceptance expires. By default a moderate risk can be accepted for up to 24 months, a high one for 12, and a critical one for 6. If you may not accept a risk, its page says why and what is needed. An acceptance can carry conditions , the things that must stay true while it runs. An acceptance covers the rating that was accepted. If the residual rating la

title: The register
heading: Seeing the whole
text: Register lists risks, with filters for category, residual rating, standing, and unit, a switch for the ones you are named on, and grouping by category or unit. Heat map places every rated risk on the matrix, for the residual, inherent, or target rating, for a unit and everything beneath it, or for one category. Each cell opens the risks in it. Reports → Risk shows where the register stands, and Reports → Compliance how ready each scope is against what it is held to. Every figure opens the list it counts. See Read the dashboards . ⌘K (or Ctrl K) finds any record by name or reference. What you see in all of these is what you are allowed to see. See Who sees what .

title: Compliance
heading: Compliance
text: Compliance This guide is for the people who answer for what the organization is held to: a security or compliance lead, the stewards of the units that must comply, and whoever reads the result. It covers frameworks, mapping controls to requirements, scopes, inherited controls, readiness, and the compliance dashboard. The idea is test once, satisfy many . A control is described once. It is mapped to every requirement it helps to meet, in as many frameworks as apply. It is tested once. What that test finds shows against every one of those requirements, in every scope that relies on the control.

title: Compliance
heading: Frameworks
text: A framework is any source of requirements: a federal rule, a security standard, the terms of a data use agreement, an internal standard. Compliance → Frameworks lists the ones on record. A new installation has four, each built from its publisher's own machine-readable file and carried as published: Framework What it is NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 Six functions, their categories, and 106 outcomes NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 The full control catalog, with the Low, Moderate, High, and Privacy baselines NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 The requirements for protecting controlled unclassified information HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C, with its standards and implementation specifications Each

title: Compliance
heading: A framework of your own
text: An agreement's terms, a sponsor's security requirements, or an internal standard is entered as a framework and then behaves like any other. Frameworks → Add a framework (a manager for the whole organization, or an administrator). Give it a title and say what kind it is, then add its requirements: one at a time, with a code, a title, and the text; by Paste , a line each: a code, a space, then what it requires; by Import , from a spreadsheet saved as CSV with a code, a title, the text, and the code of the requirement each sits under. Paste and Import check everything first and add nothing unless every line can be added. A published framework is never edited; one of your own always can be, and

title: Compliance
heading: Map controls to requirements
text: A mapping says that a control helps to satisfy a requirement, in full or in part , with a note if it needs one. From a control, open its Requirements tab: it lists what the control answers, in every framework, and adds more. From a requirement, open it in its framework: it lists the controls that answer it, and adds one. A control started from the library of common controls arrives already mapped: 46 of the 75 carry suggested mappings to the built-in frameworks. The other 29 are about things no security framework asks for, such as cold storage, research integrity, and finance. Between them the 46 answer 80 of the Cybersecurity Framework's 106 outcomes, 72 of the 97 requirements of SP 800-171

title: Compliance
heading: Scopes
text: A scope is a boundary that must meet one or more frameworks: the clinical systems, a data enclave, central computing, the whole organization. Compliance → Scopes → Add a scope (a steward of the unit, or a manager). A scope says four things. What is inside it. On Overview → Inside the boundary , list the units, processes, systems, information assets, and third parties it covers. What it is held to. Held to → Add a framework. Start from every requirement, or from a baseline where the framework has them. Which requirements apply. On the Requirements tab, every requirement applies until someone says otherwise. Leave out takes one out, and needs a reason; Bring back returns it. Only the departure

title: Compliance
heading: Inherited controls
text: A central team runs backup, identity, and the network once, for everyone. A scope that provides controls says so: edit it and tick Offers its controls to other scopes . Another scope then uses Controls → Inherit a control , and chooses how: How What it means Inherited The provider does all of it. The control stands in this scope exactly where it stands in theirs, and slips the day theirs does Shared The provider does part and this scope does the rest. It says what its part is and where that stands, and the control is as far along as the weaker half People in the inheriting scope see whose control they rely on, where it stands, and how well it is known to work, without being able to open the

title: Compliance
heading: Readiness
text: For a scope and a framework, each requirement that applies is in exactly one state. It is worked out and never typed in. title: Evidence and testing
heading: Evidence and testing
text: Evidence and testing This guide is for the people who collect proof that a control is done, and for those who test whether it works: control owners, assessors, and whoever leads an assessment. It covers evidence, its dates, files, assessments, tests, independence, and what a result changes.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Evidence
text: An evidence item is something that shows a control is done. It is collected once and attached to everything it supports. Kind What it is A file A report, an export, a screenshot, a signed form A link Where the proof lives in another system A note of what was seen What somebody looked at, and what they saw An attestation A named person's statement that something is so Compliance → Evidence → Add evidence , or Add evidence on a control or a scope, which attaches it there as it is made. Anyone may add evidence for a unit they work in, because the people who do the work hold the proof. Every item has an owner, the date it was collected, the period it covers, a data class, and the date it holds u

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Evidence stops counting
text: Evidence is true of a moment. An item holds for twelve months from the day it was collected unless you give another date, and it is in one of three states: State Meaning Current It counts Expires soon It counts, and its date is within 30 days. Its owner sees it on Home No longer counts Its date has passed. It stays on the record, and counts toward nothing Stale evidence is never deleted and never quietly renewed. Collect it again and add a new item; the old one remains as what was true then.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Attach it
text: An item counts once it is attached to the control it shows. On the item, Supports → Edit lists the controls and scopes it is attached to. One item can support many: the same restore log may be evidence for a backup control and for the scope that relies on it. Putting evidence on a control or a scope is for those who keep or assess that control or scope. Collecting is open; attaching is not.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Files
text: A file is checked by what it contains, not by its name. PDF, common images, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint documents, and plain text (including CSV and JSON) are taken, up to 25 MB. Programs are refused. Files are stored under the SHA-256 of their content, in the data home, in a directory the server does not serve from. The same file sent twice is kept once. A file only ever leaves as a download. A page or a drawing kept as evidence of a configuration is stored and returned as the plain text it is, so it cannot run in the browser. Every download is recorded in the item's history.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Who sees evidence
text: Evidence is more closely held than the register. An item is seen by whoever collected it, those named on it, and those with a role over its unit. Others see it only through something it is attached to that they may see, and not at all if it is restricted or of the most sensitive data class. A person who cannot see a control cannot download its evidence.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Assessments
text: An assessment is a planned look at whether a scope's controls work. Compliance → Assessments → Start an assessment (an assessor or a manager), or Start an assessment on a scope. Give it a name, the scope, a period, and a lead. It plans a test for each control the scope does itself: every one of them; or with Against set to a framework, only those that answer a requirement of it that applies in the scope. A control the scope inherits is not tested here. It is tested where it is provided, once, and the result reaches every scope that relies on it.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Plan the tests
text: Each test has a method (examine records and settings, interview the people who do it, or test it and see), a procedure , and a person it is assigned to . Plan on a test changes them. A test that is assigned appears on that person's Home, due on the last day of the assessment's period.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Record a result
text: Record result on a test: Design : would it reduce the risk, if it operated as described? Operation : does it operate as described? What was looked at : the sample, the period, the people asked. What was found. This is required. Evidence : cite the items that show it. Each of design and operation is effective, partly effective, or ineffective. The control is as strong as the weaker of the two.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Independence, and a second pair of eyes
text: Two rules always hold, and the server enforces both. Nobody records or reviews a result for a control they own. The test is shown to them as theirs, with someone else to do it. A result counts only when a second person has confirmed it. Whoever recorded it cannot confirm it. Recording a result changes nothing. It waits, and the assessment's lead sees it on Home. Review then either confirms it or returns it with a note saying what needs another look. A returned result is recorded again; the earlier one stays in the assessment's history.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: What a confirmed result changes
text: Confirming a result does three things at once. It becomes the control's rating , on the basis of a test, in the tester's name. It moves every requirement the control answers, in every scope that relies on it. Effective, with evidence that still counts, makes them verified. Partly effective or ineffective makes them failing, in the scope that does the control and in every scope that inherits it. It moves the residual rating that the controls suggest for every risk the control reduces. If the suggestion is now worse than the rating on record, the risk is flagged as in doubt and its owner is asked to assess again. A result of partly effective or ineffective also opens an issue for the control's

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Finish
text: Complete closes an assessment once every test in it has a result that counts. A test that will not be done is taken out first. Cancel it abandons an assessment; results already confirmed still count. The assessment's History tab tells every test planned, every result recorded, and every confirmation and return, with who did each.

title: Evidence and testing
heading: Verified, in practice
text: A requirement is verified when each control that answers it in the scope is in place, has a confirmed test result of effective that still holds, and has current evidence, either attached to the control or cited by that result. So the working rhythm for a control owner and an assessor is: The owner keeps the control's evidence current, renewing it before its date. The assessor tests the control once a year and cites that evidence. A second assessor confirms the result. Miss the first and the requirement drops to in place when the evidence goes stale. Miss the second and it drops when the test is a year old. Neither needs anyone to notice: the scope's Requirements tab and the compliance dashbo

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Issues and exceptions
text: Issues and exceptions This guide is for whoever has to put something right, whoever checks that it was, and whoever decides when a departure is allowed for a while. It covers the issue register, severity and dates, actions, closure, exceptions, the plan of action, and notices.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Issues
text: An issue is something found to be wrong that must be put right. Compliance → Issues is one register for all of them, whatever found them: Found by For example A test An assessment found a control partly effective or ineffective A gap A requirement that nothing answers in a scope Security testing A penetration test, a scan, or an exercise An audit A finding from an internal or external audit An incident Something that went wrong showed it A review A review of a supplier, a system, or a process An observation Somebody noticed it and said so

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Raise an issue
text: Issues → Raise an issue. Anyone may raise one for a unit they work in or have a role over. Say what is wrong, in which unit, how serious it is, what found it, and what it is about: the controls, scopes, and risks concerned. Name who is to put it right; they are told. On a scope's Requirements tab, Raise an issue beside a requirement that is a gap, planned, or failing starts one already about that requirement and that scope.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: From a failed test
text: When a test result of partly effective or ineffective is confirmed, an issue is opened without anyone asking: it is named for the control and the assessment, and carries what the test found and what was looked at; it is high if the control was found ineffective and moderate if partly effective; it belongs to the control's owners, who are told, and not to whoever found it; it names every scope that relies on the control. If an issue is already open for that control from an earlier test, that one stands and no second one is opened. If the control has no owner the issue has none either, and shows on Home for those who can name one.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Severity sets the date
text: Each severity has a written meaning, shown as you choose, and the issue is due a fixed time after it was raised: Severity Due within Critical 30 days High 90 days Moderate 180 days Low 365 days The table is part of the program and can be changed (see Running the program ). Changing an issue's severity applies the rule again, counted from the day it was raised. Move the date changes it by hand. That needs a reason, and where the date started and every move stay on the record, with a count beside the date wherever the issue is listed.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Put it right
text: An issue is worked through actions , each with an owner and a date: the same actions treatment plans use, on the same list of everything owed. Add an action on the issue. Whoever owns an action sees the issue, does their part, and marks it done.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Close it
text: Its owner chooses Propose closure , and says what was done, why it happened (a root cause from a short list: procedure, people and time, ownership, technology, design, change, third party, or other), and cites the evidence that shows it. Open actions must be finished or cancelled first. The issue then waits. An assessor or a manager for the unit sees it on Home and chooses Confirm closure : either confirming, which closes it, or sending it back with a note saying what is still missing. Nobody confirms the closure of an issue they own, or one they proposed closing. The server refuses it. Two more things belong to the second line alone: Withdraw , for an issue raised in error, and Reopen , for

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Who sees an issue
text: An issue is known to those with a part in it: whoever raised it, those named on it, anyone with an action on it, and those with a role over its unit. Working in the unit is not enough. An issue can also be marked restricted.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Exceptions
text: An exception is an approved departure from a control or a requirement, for a time, with what makes up for it. It is the honest answer when something cannot be met yet and everyone knows it.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Ask
text: An exception is asked for from a scope, by those who keep it: on the Requirements tab, Ask for an exception beside a requirement that is a gap, planned, or failing; on the Controls tab, Exception beside a control, including one the scope inherits and cannot fix itself. Say why it is needed, what is done in its place meanwhile, and the dates it runs between. It is never open-ended: by default it runs for at most twelve months.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Decide
text: A leader or a manager with authority over the unit decides, and whoever asked does not decide . They see the request on Home. Approving may shorten it; refusing needs a reason. Asking changes nothing: an exception covers nothing until it is approved.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: While it is in force, and after
text: While an exception is in force, what it covers is shown as excepted in place of failing, a gap, or planned, with the state underneath said beside it. It does not improve on a control that is in place. The day after it ends, the state underneath is back, without anyone doing anything. Nothing has to run for that to happen: whether an exception is in force is worked out from its dates on the day. Whoever asked sees it on Home a month before it ends. Ask again starts a new request that carries on from it, which is decided again. End it early withdraws one that is no longer needed. Compliance → Exceptions lists them, and can show those waiting to be decided, in force, ended, refused, or withdraw

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: The plan of action
text: A scope's Plan of action tab lists the open issues that bear on it: those about the scope itself, and those about any control it uses or inherits. They are listed most severe first, each with its owner, its milestones (the actions, with who and when), and its date. It prints, and it is the document a reviewer asks for: what is wrong, who is fixing it, and by when.

title: Issues and exceptions
heading: Notices
text: The bell at the top right counts what has been assigned to you or decided for you since you last looked: an issue handed to you, an action that is yours, a closure sent back, an exception approved or refused, a request waiting for your decision. A notice is a sentence and a place to go. It is not the record of what happened, which is in the history, and nobody is told about what they did themselves. Home remains the list of what you still owe.

title: Running the program
heading: Running the program
text: Running the program This guide is for the risk, compliance, and security assurance team and for administrators. It covers roles and scope, who sees what, shaping the program, the dashboards, the history, and appearance.

title: Running the program
heading: Two kinds of authority
text: RiskWren keeps administration and judgment apart. An administrator manages accounts, units, appearance, and system settings. That role reads the register and can set the program's rules, since it sets everything else up. It does not assess, rate, or accept. A manager runs the program: shapes the categories, appetite, and scoring method, edits any record, and reads everything. A manager does not accept risk either. Acceptance belongs to leaders. Someone who does both jobs holds both roles, and the history shows which they acted under.

title: Running the program
heading: Roles and scope
text: Four roles can be limited to a unit, and then cover that unit and everything beneath it: manager, assessor, leader, and steward. A manager or assessor with no unit covers the whole organization, and only a manager for the whole organization shapes the program. Capability Member Owner Steward Leader Assessor Manager Auditor Admin See what is assigned to them; finish their actions ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Read the inventory ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Read risks and controls by setting ✓ in scope in scope in scope ✓ ✓ ✓ Add a record to a unit ✓ ✓ Edit a record; link and unlink ✓ ✓ ✓ Assess a risk; rate a control ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Record a response; run a treatment plan ✓ ✓ ✓ Accept a risk ✓ not their own, up to their limit

title: Running the program
heading: Who sees what
text: The inventory is open. Processes, systems, third parties, and information assets are visible to everyone signed in, because a record can only be linked to what its author can see. So are frameworks and their requirements. The register follows a setting. A register of risks and controls is useful in proportion to how widely it is read, and sensitive in proportion to how widely it is exposed. Admin → Program → Who sees the register sets what a person with no role sees: Setting A member sees Open Every risk and control that is not restricted Unit (the default) The risks and controls of the units they belong to, and any they are named on Assigned Only the risks and controls they are named on Wha

title: Running the program
heading: Shape the program
text: Admin → Program shows how risks are rated here, in full: the categories and their appetite, the matrix, what follows from each rating, and the written definition of every level. Anyone assessing a risk sees the same definitions as they choose.

title: Running the program
heading: Appetite
text: Appetite is the highest residual rating the organization will live with for a kind of risk without a plan or an acceptance. It is set for each of the nine top categories and can be set differently for any category beneath; one that sets none takes its parent's. As shipped, clinical, regulatory, and financial risk have a low appetite, strategic risk a high one, and the rest moderate. Change any of them on the Program page. The page says at once how many risks changed standing, and the change is recorded in the history.

title: Running the program
heading: Who may accept what
text: The table on the Program page shows, for each rating, how often a risk is reviewed and who may accept it when it is above appetite: Residual rating Reviewed every May be accepted Low 24 months No acceptance is needed Moderate 12 months For up to 24 months, by a leader of the unit or above High 6 months For up to 12 months, by a leader whose limit reaches high Critical 3 months For up to 6 months, by a leader whose limit reaches critical A leader's limit is set with the role. A sensible start: unit leaders at moderate, division leaders at high, and one or two executives at critical.

title: Running the program
heading: Clocks for issues and exceptions
text: Two more rules are part of the program: Rule As shipped How long after it is raised an issue is due, by severity Critical 30 days, high 90, moderate 180, low 365 The longest an exception may run 12 months How long a control's rating, a test result, and evidence hold 12 months They are in the program pack under cadences , as issue_due_days , exception_max_months , and control_rating_months . The meanings of the four severities, the root causes an issue is closed with, what can find an issue, and the other systems a record can be known in (each with an optional address pattern, so that an identifier becomes a link) are vocabularies in the same pack.

title: Running the program
heading: Change the program with a pack
text: The scoring method, cadences, the acceptance table, and the vocabularies (kinds of system, data classes, owner kinds, and so on) are held as one document, a program pack . uv run riskwren program export --output program.json # write the one in force uv run riskwren program import program.json --dry-run # check an edited one uv run riskwren program import program.json # load it An import checks the whole pack first and reports every problem together. A scoring method in which a rating falls as likelihood or impact rises is refused. A changed method becomes a new version: assessments already made keep the version they were made under, so an old rating always means what it meant. A pack is also

title: Running the program
heading: Read the dashboards
text: There are two, each for the whole organization or for one unit and everything beneath it. Reports → Compliance shows how ready each scope is against what it is held to and what stands in the way; it is described in The compliance dashboard . Reports → Risk shows where the register stands: Figure Counts Open risks Risks that are not closed Above appetite Open risks whose residual rating exceeds the appetite for their category Need a decision Those above appetite with neither a plan on time nor an acceptance in force Reviews overdue Open risks past their next review date Ratings in doubt Risks flagged because what is known about their controls got worse Actions overdue Open actions past their

title: Running the program
heading: The history
text: Every change to every record is written to an append-only history in the same transaction as the change: who, when, and each value before and after. Each event is hashed together with the one before it, and the database itself refuses updates and deletes on the history. Each record's History tab shows its own events in plain words. Reports → History shows every change in one place, for managers, auditors, and administrators: narrowed to a person, a record, a kind of record, or a span of dates. It opens on changes to records; sign-ins, exports, and settings are one choice away. Reading is recorded where it matters: every download of an evidence file and every export of a list is an event, wit

title: Running the program
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance makes the product yours, with a live preview: the product's name and your organization's name; a logo for light and for dark mode, and a tab icon; the default palette (Wren, Slate, or Garnet) and an accent color, which is adjusted for dark mode and refused if text on it could not be read; how ratings are colored: an ordinal ramp from light to dark in one hue, which keeps rating apart from the colors of standing, or a signal ramp from green to red. Each person chooses light, dark, or system mode and a palette for themselves, from the appearance button at the top right.

title: Running the program
heading: Back up and recover
text: Back up the data home, and the database as well if you use PostgreSQL. Evidence files are in the data home under files/ , and the database refers to them. uv run riskwren program export keeps a copy of the program you have shaped. If nobody can sign in, riskwren users adds an administrator or resets a password from the server's own command line. Changes made there are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Configuration
heading: Configuration
text: Configuration This guide is for whoever runs the server. It covers riskwren.toml , environment overrides, the data home, PostgreSQL, running behind a reverse proxy, and the guard on demo installations.

title: Configuration
heading: What is configured where
text: RiskWren keeps two kinds of settings apart. Kind Where it lives Examples How the server runs riskwren.toml and the environment Address, port, database, data home The program and the product's look The database, set in the app or by a program pack Risk categories, appetite, the scoring method, cadences, vocabularies, name, logo, colors This guide is about the first. For the second, see Running the program .

title: Configuration
heading: Where the file is found
text: uv run riskwren init writes a commented riskwren.toml in the current directory. Every command looks for the file in this order: The --config FILE option (short form -c ), given before the command. The RISKWREN_CONFIG environment variable. ./riskwren.toml . uv run riskwren --config /etc/riskwren/riskwren.toml doctor Relative paths in the file are resolved against the file's own directory, not the directory you run from. An installation therefore moves as a unit.

title: Configuration
heading: Every section and key
text: The file has three sections. A section or key that RiskWren does not know is an error, not something it ignores. Every problem in the file is reported together.

title: Configuration
heading: [server]
text: Key Default Meaning host "127.0.0.1" The address the web server listens on. Keep 127.0.0.1 when a reverse proxy on the same machine terminates TLS. Use 0.0.0.0 only behind one port 8000 The port workers 1 How many server processes to run. One is enough for SQLite and small teams base_url "" The public address people use to reach RiskWren, such as "https://riskwren.example.org" . Meant for links in messages RiskWren sends. This release sends no email, so it can stay empty session_idle_hours 12 A sign-in ends after this long without activity session_max_days 7 A sign-in ends after this long in any case host , port , and workers can also be given to uv run riskwren serve as --host , --port , an

title: Configuration
heading: [database]
text: Key Default Meaning url "" Empty means SQLite, in a file inside the data home. For PostgreSQL, an address beginning postgresql+psycopg:// . See Use PostgreSQL

title: Configuration
heading: [data]
text: Key Default Meaning home "var" The data home: the one directory that holds everything not in the database RiskWren also gives advice that does not stop it running. serve and doctor warn when several workers share one SQLite file, and when base_url is http:// on a host other than localhost.

title: Configuration
heading: Environment overrides
text: Any value can be overridden by an environment variable named RISKWREN_<SECTION>_<KEY> , in capitals. The environment wins over the file. Variable Overrides RISKWREN_SERVER_HOST [server] host RISKWREN_SERVER_PORT [server] port RISKWREN_SERVER_WORKERS [server] workers RISKWREN_SERVER_BASE_URL [server] base_url RISKWREN_SERVER_SESSION_IDLE_HOURS [server] session_idle_hours RISKWREN_SERVER_SESSION_MAX_DAYS [server] session_max_days RISKWREN_DATABASE_URL [database] url RISKWREN_DATA_HOME [data] home RISKWREN_SERVER_PORT=8080 uv run riskwren serve RISKWREN_CONFIG is separate: it names the file itself.

title: Configuration
heading: Secrets are refused in the file
text: riskwren.toml is meant to be safe to read, copy, and keep under version control. RiskWren refuses to start if the file holds a secret: a key that looks like a password, secret, token, or key, or a database address with a password in it. Put secrets in the environment instead. For the database, set the password in PGPASSWORD , or put the whole address, password and all, in RISKWREN_DATABASE_URL .

title: Configuration
heading: The data home
text: The data home is created by init . With the default settings it is ./var . Path Holds The SQLite database When no database address is set brand/ Uploaded logos and the tab icon logs/ The server's log, rotated files/ Evidence files, each stored once under the SHA-256 of its content. Nothing here is served directly exports/ Reserved for exports .riskwren-home A marker that says this directory is a data home Back it up as a whole. With PostgreSQL, back up the database as well. Do not edit its contents by hand. It must be writable by the account that runs the server. Request bodies and tokens are never written to the log.

title: Configuration
heading: Use PostgreSQL
text: SQLite is the default and needs no setup. Use PostgreSQL when many people will use RiskWren at once or you want more than one server process. The features and the data model are the same on both, and the test suite runs on both. Install the driver, which is optional: `` bash uv sync --extra postgres `` Create an empty database and a role that owns it, with your usual PostgreSQL tools. Set the address in riskwren.toml , without the password: `` toml [database] url = "postgresql+psycopg://riskwren@db.example.org:5432/riskwren" `` Put the password in the environment, then set up and check: `` bash export PGPASSWORD=… uv run riskwren init uv run riskwren doctor `` Moving an existing installation

title: Configuration
heading: Upgrade
text: After updating the code: uv sync uv run riskwren db upgrade db upgrade applies any migrations the database has not had and adds anything new in the default program without overwriting what you have shaped. Coming from 0.1.0, that is the four public frameworks and the mappings the common controls carry to them; your own controls are not mapped for you, and each one that came from the library offers the mappings on its Requirements tab. Back up first: an upgrade cannot be undone except by restoring. serve refuses to start on a schema that is behind, and uv run riskwren db current shows where the database is.

title: Configuration
heading: Run behind a reverse proxy
text: RiskWren speaks plain HTTP and expects a reverse proxy to terminate TLS in front of it. Keep host = "127.0.0.1" when the proxy is on the same machine. Have the proxy send X-Forwarded-Proto: https . RiskWren marks its session cookie Secure when the request arrived over HTTPS, by that header or directly. Forward the Host header unchanged. Requests that change anything are refused when their origin does not match the host, which is part of the protection against requests from other sites. Requests larger than 32 MB are refused. The app sets its own security headers, including a content security policy with no inline script or style and no third-party origins, so the proxy does not need to add t

title: Configuration
heading: The demo and the network
text: A demo organization signs in anyone who asks as any of its sample people, with no password. So a demo's server listens only on the machine it runs on: serve refuses any other host, and the sample sign-in refuses requests from other machines. If you do want to show a demo to others on a network you trust: uv run riskwren --config demo/riskwren.toml serve --host 0.0.0.0 --demo-on-network Anyone who can reach it can then sign in as the demo's risk manager or administrator. Never do this with a database that holds anything real; a demo database holds nothing that is.

title: The API
heading: The API
text: API Everything the web app does, it does through a JSON API under /api/v1 . This guide covers how to sign in, how answers and errors are shaped, how lists page, and what routes there are. The exact shape of every request and answer is in the OpenAPI document: openapi.json in this directory, or /api/openapi.json on a running server. This release has no API tokens. A program signs in as an account, with that account's password, and holds a session as a browser does. Tokens scoped to a role arrive with integrations in a later release; see the roadmap . Until 1.0, routes may change between releases. Changes are listed in the changelog .

title: The API
heading: Sign in
text: curl -s -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"email": "you@example.org", "password": "…"}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/session The answer describes who you are, and sets a session cookie, riskwren_session : { "data": { "account": {"id": 12, "name": "Your Name", "email": "you@example.org"}, "roles": ["manager"], "permissions": {"…": true}, "units": {"manager": null}, "member_units": [4], "has_password": true, "csrf_token": "…" }, "meta": {} } In units , each scoped role lists the units it covers, or null for the whole organization. GET /api/v1/session returns the same for the session you hold, or 401 if you hold none. DELETE /api/v1/session signs out.

title: The API
heading: Changing things
text: Every request that changes anything ( POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE ) must carry the session's CSRF token in a header: curl -s -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'X-CSRF-Token: …' \ -d '{"name": "Freezer farm", "kind": "device", "criticality": "critical", "org_unit_id": 4}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/systems Without it the answer is 403. If the request carries an Origin header, it must match the host, or the request is refused.

title: The API
heading: Editing a record someone else is editing
text: Records carry a version . Send the version you read with a PATCH , and if someone else has changed the record since, the answer is 409 and nothing is saved. Read it again and decide what to do.

title: The API
heading: Answers
text: Every successful answer has the same envelope: {"data": …, "meta": {…}} data is one object or a list. meta carries what is about the answer and not in it: paging for a list, or a count of what else changed. Times are UTC in ISO 8601. Dates with no time, such as a due date, are YYYY-MM-DD .

title: The API
heading: Errors
text: Errors are problem documents ( application/problem+json ): { "type": "about:blank", "title": "Unprocessable Entity", "status": 422, "detail": "The assessment was not recorded.", "errors": [ {"location": ["rationale"], "message": "Say why, in a sentence or two. A rating is a judgment."} ], "instance": "/api/v1/risks/RSK-0002/assessments" } Status Meaning 400 The request could not be carried out as asked 401 Nobody is signed in, or the email address and password do not match 403 You are signed in but may not do this, or the CSRF token is missing. detail says which 404 No such thing, or none that you may see. The two are not told apart 409 A conflict: the record changed since you read it, or th

title: The API
heading: Lists
text: Every list route takes the same parameters: Parameter Meaning q Words to look for in the name, reference, or summary, or in what the record is called in another system unit A unit's id. Includes every unit beneath it sort A field name. Start with - for descending. The default is -updated_at limit How many to return: 50 by default, 200 at most cursor Where to continue from: next_cursor or prev_cursor from the last answer mine true for only the records you are named on Each kind of record adds its own filters, such as standing , residual_rating , and category for risks. The OpenAPI document lists them. A list's meta says where the page sits: {"total": 180, "offset": 0, "next_cursor": "eyJvZmZz

title: The API
heading: Routes
text: Every route requires a signed-in account except those marked public. What a route allows beyond that depends on the record: its unit, its owners, and its visibility. See Running the program .

title: The API
heading: System and session
text: Route What it does GET /health/live · GET /health/ready Whether the server is up, and whether it can serve (public) GET /meta Product name, version, branding, and palettes (public) GET · POST · DELETE /session Who is signed in; sign in; sign out POST /session/password Change your own password

title: The API
heading: People and units

title: The API
heading: What the API will not do
text: It never returns a record you may not see, and never counts one. It never edits an assessment, a control rating, a test result, or an acceptance. Each is superseded by a new one. It never lets a person record or confirm a test result for a control they own, confirm the closure of an issue they own, or decide an exception they asked for. It never imports a rating. A file can say what a risk or a control is, and not how it has been judged. It never changes the history. There is no route that does.

title: Command reference
heading: Command reference
text: Command reference Every riskwren command. This page is written from the program itself, so it always matches the version it ships with. Run commands with uv run riskwren … from the project directory. Options that come before the command apply to all of them: riskwren [-h] [--version] [-c FILE] [-v | -q] COMMAND ...

title: Command reference
heading: Commands
text: Command What it does riskwren init Set up a new installation riskwren serve Run the web server riskwren demo Build a fictional organization to explore riskwren db Look after the database schema riskwren users Manage accounts from the command line riskwren verify Check that the history has not been altered riskwren frameworks See and load what the organization is held to riskwren program Move the program between installations riskwren doctor Check that this installation is healthy

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren init
text: Write a configuration file if there is none, create the data home, create or upgrade the database, and create the first administrator if there is none. Safe to run again. Option Meaning --force overwrite an existing configuration file --admin-email EMAIL create the first administrator with this address --admin-name NAME the first administrator's name --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren serve
text: Run RiskWren's web server. It refuses to start on a database whose schema is behind; run riskwren db upgrade first. Option Meaning --host address to listen on (default: from the configuration) --port PORT port to listen on (default: from the configuration) --workers WORKERS server processes (default: from the configuration) --reload restart when the code changes (development) --demo-on-network let a demo organization listen beyond this machine (anyone who reaches it can sign in as its sample people)

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren demo
text: Build the Northmere Institute for Health Research, a fictional organization with two years of history, in its own directory. Everything in it is made by the same code the app uses. Start it with the command it prints. Option Meaning PATH where to build it (default: ./demo) --seed SEED a different number gives a different Northmere --port PORT the port its server will use (default: 8020) --force rebuild a demo that is already there

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren db
text: Look after the database schema.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren db upgrade
text: Apply any migrations the database has not had. Export first: an upgrade cannot be undone except by restoring.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren db current
text: Show which migration the database is at, and which this version expects. Exits with 1 when they differ.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users
text: Manage accounts from the command line: for setting up, and for getting back in when nobody can sign in. Everyday account management is in the app, under Admin. Changes made here are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users add
text: Add an account. It asks for a password unless --password-stdin or --invite is given. Option Meaning EMAIL the email address the person signs in with --name the person's name --title their job title --role ROLE a role: admin, manager, assessor, auditor, steward=unit:CODE, or leader=unit:CODE,limit:RATING; manager and assessor may also take unit:CODE (may be repeated) --unit CODE a unit they work in, by code (may be repeated) --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking --invite add them without a password: they can be named on records now, and sign in once they are given a password or use single sign-on

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users list
text: List every account with its status and roles.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users disable
text: Stop an account signing in and end its sessions. Its records and history are kept. The last active administrator cannot be disabled. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users enable
text: Let a disabled account sign in again. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users reset-password
text: Give an account a new password and end its sessions. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren users roles
text: Show an account's roles, or with --set replace the roles granted in RiskWren. Roles mapped from an identity provider are left alone. The last active administrator cannot lose that role. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address --set ROLE a role: admin, manager, assessor, auditor, steward=unit:CODE, or leader=unit:CODE,limit:RATING; manager and assessor may also take unit:CODE (may be repeated); with none, removes every role

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren verify
text: Recompute the hash chain over every event in the history and report the first one that does not hold. Exits with 1 if the history is broken.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren frameworks
text: A framework is a source of requirements: a public standard, a regulation, an agreement's terms. Four public ones ship with RiskWren and are loaded at installation. Others are loaded from a pack file, or entered in the app.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren frameworks list
text: List every framework.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren frameworks load
text: Load a framework from a pack file, or the built-in ones that are missing. A pack is checked whole first and refused whole if anything is wrong. Option Meaning FILE the pack to load --builtin load the built-in frameworks not yet here --dry-run check the pack, and load nothing

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren frameworks show
text: Show a framework's publisher, version, license, and source. Option Meaning KEY the framework's key, such as nist-csf

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren program
text: The program is everything a risk and compliance team configures: vocabularies, the risk categories and their appetite, the scoring method, cadences, and who may accept what. It lives in the database and moves as one file.

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren program export
text: Write the whole program as one JSON document, to a file or to standard output. Option Meaning --output , -o FILE write to this file

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren program import
text: Load a program pack. The whole pack is checked first, and nothing is loaded unless all of it can be. A new scoring method is published as a new version; assessments already made keep the version they were made under. Option Meaning FILE the pack to load --dry-run say what would change, and change nothing

title: Command reference
heading: riskwren doctor
text: Check the configuration, the data home, the database and its schema, and the history. Exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.
